name: Junmai ginjo and junmai daiginjo (pure-rice ginjo grades)
ja: 純米吟醸・純米大吟醸
text: Two of the eight tokutei meisho-shu classes, both made from rice and rice koji only, with no brewers' alcohol. The sources give a rice polishing ratio of 60 percent or less for junmai ginjo and 50 percent or less for junmai daiginjo. The ratio is the share of the grain that remains after milling, so a smaller number means harder milling. The legal text is an NTA labelling notice; the sources here are retail and brewer explainers that summarise it.
flavor: Heard on every sake list and bottle front label; shorthand for the top pure-rice tier.
use: Junmai daiginjo is the 50-percent-or-less pure-rice class and junmai ginjo the 60-percent-or-less one; a shop will pour them as the premium by-the-glass tier or pair them with delicate raw fish.
craft: The percentage is a ceiling, not a quality guarantee. Many labels print a lower figure than the legal limit, so read the actual seimai-buai instead of inferring it from the class name. Junmai in the name only tells you there was no jozo alcohol.

name: Tokubetsu junmai (special pure-rice sake)
text: A tokutei meisho-shu class made from rice and rice koji only. According to the sources it carries the word tokubetsu when the polishing ratio is 60 percent or less, or when a special production method is declared on the label. Unlike junmai ginjo it is not tied to ginjo-style brewing. A junmai with no polishing-ratio requirement exists as a separate plain junmai class.
flavor: Heard when a brewery's standard pure-rice bottle is a notch above its basic junmai.
use: Listed on menus and labels as the mid-priced pure-rice pour, often the brewery's house everyday-premium sake.
craft: The word 'special' has two possible triggers, a 60 percent ratio or a stated special method, so always check the back label to see which one the brewery used. The explanation is mandatory for the method route. Don't assume it is milled to 60 percent just because it says tokubetsu.

name: Tokubetsu honjozo (special honjozo, with brewers' alcohol)
text: A tokutei meisho-shu class made from rice, rice koji and brewers' alcohol. The sources give the same two triggers for the word tokubetsu as for tokubetsu junmai: a polishing ratio of 60 percent or less, or a special production method stated on the label. Plain honjozo is listed at 70 percent or less. The alcohol-added classes are the other half of the eight-class system, alongside the four pure-rice classes.
flavor: Heard in izakaya sake lists and brewery line-ups as a drier, cleaner everyday grade.
use: Used for warm service and as an all-round table sake; named explicitly on labels in the 'tokubetsu honjozo' form.
craft: Don't equate alcohol-added with cheap. The sources describe the alcohol as added to keep the finish clean and the aroma lifted. What a buyer should still check is the declared polishing ratio and the method note.

name: Jozo arukoru (brewers' alcohol)
text: Distilled alcohol added to the moromi in the alcohol-added classes: honjozo, tokubetsu honjozo, ginjo and daiginjo. The sources describe its purpose as limiting deterioration of flavour and tidying the aftertaste, and one source gives the cap as 10 percent or less of the total weight of the raw rice. Its presence, together with the polishing ratio, is what separates a daiginjo from a junmai daiginjo.
flavor: Heard in the arguments about 'aruten' sake and in labelling discussions.
use: Used as a classification clue: pure-rice classes carry the word junmai, while alcohol-added classes list jozo alcohol among the ingredients.
craft: The 10 percent figure comes from secondary explainers; confirm the exact limit in the NTA notice before quoting it on a menu or a spec sheet. Do not describe it as a flavouring. In the sources it is added to shape lightness and finish.

name: Kojimai shiyo buai (koji rice usage ratio, 15 percent minimum)
text: A requirement for the tokutei meisho-shu classes that koji rice be at least 15 percent of the rice used. One source says this standard was added in a 2003 revision and applied from January 2004. It sits next to the polishing ratio and the alcohol rule as one of the formal conditions behind the eight class names.
flavor: Heard in technical brewing and labelling talk, rarely on a menu.
use: Used when checking whether a sake qualifies for a tokutei meisho-shu name, together with the rice polishing ratio.
craft: This figure is easy to confuse with a brewery's own koji ratio for flavour. It is a legal floor for the class, not a description of how much koji the brewer actually used. Verify the exact wording in the NTA notice, since the sources I saw are explainers and note that some details differ between them.

name: Chiriteki hyoji / GI (geographical indication) system, split between NTA and MAFF
text: Japan runs two GI tracks. Sake, wine, distilled spirits (shochu and awamori) and other liquors are designated by the National Tax Agency, not by the agriculture ministry. Foods and farm products go through MAFF's separate GI protection system. The Kinki regional bureau of MAFF explains that liquor GIs are managed outside MAFF. Kobe Beef, for example, is described as GI-registered as well as holding a regional collective trademark.
flavor: Heard when someone asks whether a name like Hakusan or Kobe Beef is 'protected' and by whom.
use: Used to tell which registry to check: NTA list for a liquor name, MAFF register for a food name.
craft: A GI is a geographic and quality-linked name protection, a different instrument from a regional collective trademark (chiiki dantai shohyo). A product can hold both. Check the register that matches the product category, as a liquor will not appear on the MAFF food list.
src: MAFF Kinki - GI and intellectual property

name: Hakusan (GI sake, first sake GI)
text: A sake geographical indication on the National Tax Agency list, designated on 22 December 2005 for Hakusan city in Ishikawa. The NTA list shows it as the earliest of the sake entries seen in these results, followed by Nihonshu (25 December 2015), Yamagata (16 December 2016) and Nadagogo (28 June 2018). The GI limits use of the place name to sake that meets the designated conditions for that area.
flavor: Heard when discussing Ishikawa sake and the origin of sake GIs.
use: Used as a reference point for how a place name on a sake label is protected, and as the oldest sake GI example.
craft: The sources here give the designation date and area but not the production conditions. Pull the conditions from the NTA GI pages before claiming anything about rice, water or brewing method for a specific GI.
src: JETRO - Kyoto, Tottori, Fukuoka sake GIs

name: Nadagogo (GI sake, the five Nada districts)
text: A sake GI designated by the National Tax Agency on 28 June 2018. The area is given as Nada ward and Higashinada ward in Kobe plus Ashiya and Nishinomiya, all in Hyogo. It sits on the same NTA list as Hakusan, Yamagata, Nihonshu and later additions such as Kyoto, Tottori and Fukuoka, which the JETRO piece reports as registered in 2025.
flavor: Heard in discussions of Hyogo sake and in how large-brewery districts are protected.
use: Used to confirm a label's Nadagogo claim against the NTA register and area list.
craft: A district GI covers a defined area, so check where the product is actually brewed. The detailed production standard is on the NTA page; I did not see it in these results, so verify before quoting it.
src: JETRO - Kyoto, Tottori, Fukuoka sake GIs

name: Nikushitsu tokyu (meat quality grade 1 to 5)
text: The second half of a beef carcass grade such as A5. The Japan Meat Grading Association scores four items: marbling, colour and lustre of the meat, firmness and texture, and colour and quality of the fat. The sources state the carcass takes the lowest of the four item grades as its meat quality grade, not an average. Grade 5 is the top.
flavor: Heard at the market and on every Japanese beef spec sheet as the number after the letter.
use: Used to specify wagyu carcass or cuts, for example 'A5' or 'A4', in purchasing and on menus.
craft: Because the lowest item decides the grade, a carcass with great marbling can still fall to 4 on a weak colour or texture item. Grade is not a flavour guarantee, so many buyers also ask the producer and breed for context.

name: BMS (beef marbling standard, No. 1 to 12)
ja: BMSナンバー(脂肪交雑基準)
text: The 12-step scale for marbling (shibo-kosa) on a beef carcass. The explainers give the mapping to meat quality grade as BMS 8 to 12 for grade 5, 5 to 7 for grade 4, 3 to 4 for grade 3, 2 for grade 2 and 1 for grade 1. Judging is done on the cross-section at the grading site between the sixth and seventh ribs.
flavor: Heard when a producer quotes 'BMS 11' or 'No. 12' for bragging-right sirloin.
use: Used on spec sheets and auction results to separate carcasses inside the single grade 5 band.
craft: Grade 5 covers BMS 8 to 12, a wide spread, so BMS is the number that separates a good A5 from an exceptional one. High marbling is not automatically ideal for every dish, and the sources say grade alone does not guarantee taste.

name: Budomari tokyu (yield grade A, B, C)
text: The letter in a beef grade. It estimates how much saleable meat a carcass yields, using a yield base value computed from ribeye area, rib thickness, carcass weight and subcutaneous fat thickness. The JMGA standard as summarised: 72 or above is A, 69 to under 72 is B, under 69 is C. It says nothing about eating quality.
flavor: Heard as the letter in A4, A5, B3 and similar carcass codes.
use: Used by buyers and butchers to estimate cutting yield and price.
craft: Yield is about quantity of meat, and one explainer states plainly that it is unrelated to taste. A chef buying for flavour should read the number, not the letter, and pay attention to the breed, feed and region.

name: A5 rank (top wagyu carcass code)
text: A5 is the top combination of the two grading axes: yield grade A and meat quality grade 5. It is assigned by the Japan Meat Grading Association's nationwide standard. Writers stress that the code is a grading result, not a guarantee of flavour, and that BMS inside grade 5 can range from 8 to 12.
flavor: Heard on menus and in retail ads as shorthand for the most marbled wagyu.
use: Used to describe carcasses and cuts, often as 'A5 wagyu'; chefs typically ask for BMS and the producer as well.
craft: A5 does not mean the best for every dish. The letter is yield, the 5 is the lowest of four quality items, and marbling can be heavier than a grilled or thin-sliced preparation wants.

name: Jidori (JAS-defined native-lineage chicken)
text: A chicken category defined in the JAS standard for jidori meat. As the sources summarise it: chicks with at least 50 percent native-breed lineage and a birth record, raised on the floor from day 28, at no more than 10 birds per square metre. Most sources say at least 80 days from hatching, though one reports 75 days, so read the JAS text. One source says jidori is about 1 percent of chicken in distribution.
flavor: Heard on yakitori menus and supplier sheets to signal firm, flavourful bird.
use: Used as a strict category: only birds meeting the requirements can be sold as jidori.
craft: The word is legally constrained, unlike meigara-dori. Ask for the breed, rearing days and farm, and note that sources disagree on days, so don't quote one number without checking the standard.

name: Meigara-dori / burando-dori (branded chicken)
text: Branded chicken with no JAS definition like jidori's. The sources describe it as broiler-based birds differentiated by feed or longer rearing, with standards set by each producer or group. One source mentions recognition by the Japan Poultry Association, but the sources do not agree on how formal that is.
flavor: Heard on supplier lists as a step above ordinary broilers, and often confused with jidori.
use: Used when a brand name, not the law, is the selling point; spec sheets usually name the brand and farm.
craft: Never write jidori for a meigara-dori. Treat each brand's own spec as the authority and ask for rearing days, feed and breed.

name: Broiler (wakadori, short-fattened young chicken)
text: The standard commodity chicken, shipped after a short fattening period. Sources typically put the rearing at around 50 to 60 days. It makes up the large majority of chicken in distribution and is the base for many branded meigara-dori. It is the baseline against which jidori and branded birds are compared.
flavor: Heard as the plain 'wakadori' or 'broiler' line on supply sheets.
use: Used for volume menu items where price and consistency matter.
craft: Short days mean softer, milder meat. When a menu promises bite and depth, specify jidori or a named brand rather than generic wakadori.

name: Kou-rui shochu (class A, continuous-distilled)
ja: 甲類焼酎(連続式蒸留焼酎)
text: A Liquor Tax Act category of shochu distilled in a continuous still. The sources give its alcohol strength as under 36 percent. Repeated distillation makes it light in character, so it is the neutral-leaning style used in mixers and chuhai. It is distinct from otsu-rui shochu, which uses a pot-type still.
flavor: Heard in izakaya for chuhai and sours, and as the 'not honkaku' side of the shochu split.
use: Used as a mixing base or for sours, not for neat service.
craft: The ko/otsu split is by still type and strength, not by quality. Don't call ko-rui a worse shochu, just a different tool.

name: Otsu-rui shochu (class B, single-distilled)
ja: 乙類焼酎(単式蒸留焼酎)
text: A Liquor Tax Act category of shochu from a pot-type still. The sources give its alcohol strength as 45 percent or less. A single distillation leaves more of the raw material's flavour, which is why imo, mugi and kome shochu come from this class. Otsu-rui is not the same as honkaku shochu, which is a label for a subset.
flavor: Heard in the same breath as honkaku shochu, and often wrongly treated as identical.
use: Used to describe pot-still shochu in tax and labelling terms.
craft: Otsu-rui is the tax class, honkaku is the label. A pot-still shochu does not automatically meet the honkaku conditions, so check the label.

name: Honkaku shochu (authentic shochu label)
text: A label used for single-distilled shochu that meets set conditions. One explainer stresses it is not just another name for otsu-rui, but a designation applied to a subset of pot-still shochu. The results here do not spell out the conditions, so check the Honkaku Shochu & Awamori association page for the exact criteria.
flavor: Heard on bottles and in trade talk as the premium, flavourful side of shochu.
use: Used on labels and menus to separate flavour-forward pot-still shochu from mixer-style ko-rui.
craft: Do not treat honkaku and otsu-rui as synonyms. Ask which conditions the label refers to, and verify against the association's classification page.

name: Arabushi (rough katsuobushi, unmolded)
text: Katsuobushi that is smoked and dried but not given the mould treatment. Sources say most commercial shaved bonito in supermarket bags is arabushi, with strong aroma and taste. It is the first stage that karebushi and honkarebushi build on.
flavor: Heard in discussions of soba tsuyu, ramen dashi and anywhere a strong smoky punch is wanted.
use: Used where strength is needed, as against honkarebushi, which suits light clear soups.
craft: Strong and smoky is the point, but it can overwhelm delicate stock. Match the grade to the dish and don't swap it one-for-one with honkarebushi.

name: Karebushi (mold-treated katsuobushi)
text: Katsuobushi that has had the mould treatment at least once. Sources disagree on counts: one says the JAS counts karebushi as finished with up to a second mould, while a shaved-bonito maker describes two rounds as the common karebushi. Treat the count as unsettled and check with the supplier.
flavor: Heard as the middle grade between arabushi and honkarebushi.
use: Used for dashi where more refinement than arabushi is wanted.
craft: Mould treatment lowers moisture and breaks down fat, which clears the flavour and removes fishiness. Because the counts vary between sources, ask how many mould rounds a given product had.

name: Honkarebushi (true dried-and-molded katsuobushi)
text: The top form of katsuobushi, repeatedly moulded and sun-dried. Sources disagree on the count: one says two to three rounds, another says four or more. The mould lowers moisture and breaks down fat, leaving a more translucent, less fishy piece. It is costly and described as suited to light clear soups.
flavor: Heard in high-end kitchens for refined, gentle dashi.
use: Used for ichiban dashi and suimono where aroma and clarity matter.
craft: The count is not agreed between sources, so verify it with the supplier rather than relying on the name alone. A honkarebushi's price comes from the labour of repeated moulding and drying.

name: Osubushi and mesubushi (male and female fillet pieces)
text: Katsuobushi is cut from a bonito into two kinds of pieces, osubushi and mesubushi. The sources I saw note that the pieces are split by cut, and one says mesubushi has more fat and suits dashi. The terms refer to the fillet cut, not to the sex of the fish.
flavor: Heard in shaved-bonito shops and when buying whole blocks.
use: Used when picking blocks: the cut, not just the mould grade, affects how a katsuobushi performs.
craft: The fat remark comes from a single source in my results, so confirm with the maker before specifying a cut for a recipe.

name: Ittoken, nitoken (kombu grade inspection, 1st and 2nd class)
ja: 一等検・二等検(昆布の等級)
text: Kombu grades are set under the Hokkaido Fisheries Product Inspection Association standard from length, width, weight, thickness, colour, damage, white powder and bundling. The number of grades varies by source, from about four to six. Many sources tie the grade to a coloured tie-cord: blue for first, red for second, purple for third, brown for fourth, though one shop says green for first.
flavor: Heard in kombu shops and dashi purchasing: 'ittoken' or 'nitoken'.
use: Used to specify kombu on orders, e.g. Makombu ittoken.
craft: Grade is mainly a sort by leaf size, thickness and condition, not a flavour ranking: a source says higher grade is not necessarily the better dashi. Cord colour reporting varies, so ask the shop for the standard it uses.

name: Hama kakusa (beach grade differences in Hidaka kombu)
text: For Hidaka kombu, quality also varies by the beach where it grew, ranked in the sources as tokujo-hama, jo-hama, chu-hama and nami-hama. The same first grade can therefore differ in quality between beaches. It is a second axis on top of the inspection grade.
flavor: Heard in kombu wholesaling when someone asks 'which hama is it from'.
use: Used by buyers to differentiate same-grade Hidaka kombu.
craft: Ask for both the grade and the hama. The ranking terms come from a single trade source in my results, so confirm them with your supplier.

name: Nagagiri and bo-kombu (cut-and-bundled kombu forms)
text: Two ways kombu is cut and bundled for trade. Per one source, nagagiri is cut to uniform lengths of 75 to 105 cm and bundled, and bo-kombu is cut to short uniform lengths of 20 to 60 cm. The form is separate from the quality grade.
flavor: Heard in kombu wholesale catalogues.
use: Used to specify pack form and length for kitchens and processors.
craft: Check the length range in the supplier's own spec, because the figures here come from one trade source. The form does not tell you the grade.

name: Yoshoku and kaito hyoji (farmed and thawed labelling)
text: Under the fresh-food labelling rules as summarised, farmed seafood must be labelled yoshoku and seafood thawed from frozen must be labelled kaito. Domestically farmed seafood also needs a region name, which means the prefecture of the main farm. The rules are in the Consumer Affairs Agency's food labelling standard.
flavor: Heard in supermarket and fishmonger sign-writing, and in restaurant inspections.
use: Used on product tags and menus where the fish was farmed or thawed.
craft: A restaurant should be able to say whether a fish is wild or farmed and fresh or thawed. The region for farmed fish is the farm's prefecture, not where it was landed.

name: Seisan suiiki-mei (production water-area labelling for seafood)
text: For domestic fresh seafood, the origin label is the water area name, or the landing port or its prefecture when the water area is hard to state. Imports show the country of origin, and a water area is optional. The Japan Fisheries Agency publishes a guideline for fresh seafood production water areas.
flavor: Heard in market tags such as 'Seto Inland Sea' or a port name.
use: Used to state where a wild fish was caught on tags and menus.
craft: Port or prefecture is acceptable as a fallback, but a water-area name tells the buyer more. Farmed fish take the farm's prefecture instead.

name: Tokubetsu saibai nosanbutsu (specially cultivated produce)
text: Produce grown under the MAFF labelling guideline in which both the number of reduced-target pesticide applications and the nitrogen from chemical fertiliser are 50 percent or less of the regional conventional level. Both reductions are required. If no pesticide was used, the label says that reduced-target pesticides were not used during the growing period. Conventional levels are set by each prefecture.
flavor: Heard on rice and vegetable labels, and often confused with organic or pesticide-free.
use: Used on produce and rice labels to state reduced-input cultivation.
craft: It is a reduction against a regional baseline, not a ban, and it differs from organic. Ask for the prefecture's baseline and the grower's actual figures if the claim matters.

name: Chiiki dantai shohyo (regional collective trademark)
text: A trademark system introduced on 1 April 2006 to protect regional brands. It allows registration of a place name combined with a product name, with a lower bar than ordinary trademarks: awareness around neighbouring prefectures is enough, and a close tie to the region is required. Eligible holders include cooperatives, chambers of commerce and NPOs.
flavor: Heard when a producer group explains how it protects a name like Kobe Beef.
use: Used for names such as Kobe Beef and Seki-aji; holders are groups, not single firms.
craft: It is a trademark, not a GI, and a product can hold both. Only the group that owns the mark can authorise its use.
src: JPO - regional collective trademark presentation (JETRO PDF)

name: Kobe Beef (regional collective trademark no. 5068214)
ja: 神戸ビーフ(地域団体商標)
text: Registered as regional collective trademark no. 5068214. The holder is the Hyogo Meat Business Cooperative Federation and the designated goods are Hyogo-origin wagyu meat. Related marks listed include Kobe Niku, Kobe Gyu, Tajima Beef and Tajima Gyu. One source says Kobe Beef is also GI-registered.
flavor: Heard as the best-known example of a protected beef name.
use: Used to illustrate how a place-name beef brand is controlled through a trademark owned by a producer federation.
craft: A name trademark is held by the federation, so use of the name is governed by that group's rules. Check the JPO entry for the exact goods covered.

name: Seki-aji (regional collective trademark no. 5005587)
text: Registered as regional collective trademark no. 5005587. It marks horse mackerel caught by pole-and-line by members of the Saganoseki branch of the Oita fisheries cooperative, shipped with a dedicated tag to set it apart and to counter fakes. It is a standard example of a catch method and landing site protected by the name.
flavor: Heard in Oita and at premium fish counters.
use: Used as a tagged, branded aji on menus and at markets.
craft: Look for the dedicated tag. The mark attaches to members' pole-and-line catch, not to any aji from the area.
